sentences: Senior barrister the old lawyer is nearing retirement after a heart attack.
He agrees to defend the client, despite the nurse's objections and the old lawyer's doctor having warned against taking stressful criminal cases.
The client is accused of murdering the victim, a wealthy, childless widow who fell in love with him and named him as the main beneficiary in her will.
Despite the evidence, the old lawyer believes his client to be innocent.

The old lawyer speaks with the client's German wife, the wife, whom he finds cold and self-possessed; she provides the client with an alibi, but the old lawyer warns her that juries often do not accept alibis given by spouses.
The old lawyer is later shocked when the wife is called to give evidence against the client as a prosecution witness.

While a wife cannot be compelled to testify against her husband, it is revealed that her marriage to the client is invalid, as she was already married to another man, the first husband, still alive and living in her homeland.
She states that she never loved the client, and her conscience compels her to tell the truth.

She explains that she met the client, an air force sergeant serving in the occupied city's British occupation zone, and went through a marriage ceremony with him solely to escape from Soviet-controlled territory.
According to her testimony, the client arrived home after the time of the murder, and openly confessed that he had killed the victim.
The old lawyer fears that his client will be convicted and sentenced to hang.
He is then unexpectedly contacted by a Cockney woman, who offers to sell him compromising letters written by the wife to a man named the correspondent.

The handwriting is genuine, and the woman appears to have a legitimate reason for providing the correspondence: the correspondent, who had once been her lover, had attacked her, leaving her with facial scars.
During cross examination, the old lawyer reads the letters, which disclose a conspiracy between the correspondent and the wife to frame the client.
The jury acquits the client.
The old lawyer admits that his victory seemed suspiciously easy, and is proved right when the wife returns to the courtroom to avoid an angry crowd waiting outside.
She explains that, after the old lawyer's earlier warnings about alibis, she had decided to pose as a hateful, double-crossing wife.
She wrote letters to a non-existent lover (the correspondent) and impersonated the disfigured woman who passed them to the old lawyer.
The wife loves the client, but knew he was guilty; she told the truth about the client's confession in the witness-box, then used the false letters to discredit her own testimony.
The old lawyer is outraged, but the law of double jeopardy prevents any renewed prosecution of the client.
The client reveals he is having an affair with a much younger woman, and intends to abandon the wife.
He smugly states that, though the wife will be tried for perjury, he and she are now even, having saved each other's lives.
A devastated wife grabs a knife and fatally stabs the client.
As she is taken into custody, the old lawyer decides to further delay his retirement to defend the wife.
Ever since his assistant the secretary went missing, private detective the investigator has been drinking and he is now homeless.
Although the investigator hasn't worked a case in seven years, his old police friend the captain asks for his assistance on a job.
The captain and the investigator were both in love with the secretary, which had ended their friendship.
The case involves a senator who has been murdered.
The investigator is needed to talk with the wounded man, a dying sailor who refuses to speak with anybody else.
According to federal agent the government man, not only has the wounded man been shot by the same gun recently used to kill a politician, he is actually an undercover federal agent.
The investigator's investigation leads to the woman, the late senator's widow.
She is beautiful and seductive, but the investigator does not trust her.
He learns that they are caught in the fallout from a network of spies operating during the world war.
Now a killer nicknamed the assassin is trying to silence people who had information about the spy operation.
The investigator finds and kills the assassin.
He confronts the woman with his suspicions about her involvement.
The woman fires a shotgun that the investigator had rigged to backfire in order to test her loyalty.
It is not clear if the secretary is still alive.
Writer the author believes a series of seemingly unrelated "accidental" deaths are linked murders.
He asks his friend the investigator, recently retired from the security service, to investigate, and provides a list of the victims' names.
Soon after, the author's plane is bombed and crashes into the sea while he is en route to collect evidence to confirm his suspicions.
With his dying breath, he tells a fellow passenger, the survivor, the key to the mystery, though his exact meaning is garbled.
The survivor survives and turns out to be the investigator's old world war counterpart in the French resistance movement.
They join forces to investigate the author's list and decode his cryptic final words.
The lady, the author's widowed cousin and a former love interest of the investigator, soon joins them.
The survivor becomes strongly attracted to the lady.
The first conclusion the investigator and the survivor draw from the author's dying words is about important information contained in his unpublished manuscript regarding his war experiences.
They go to the author's apartment, but the murderer has already been there and taken and re-typed several pages, removing key information.
He happened to encounter the lady as he was leaving, then went to murder the typist.
After inspecting the manuscript, the investigator spots the retyped page.
The lady's description of the man in the apartment differs from the survivor's, who saw the murderer at the airport.
From this, the investigator determines that the killer wears realistic masks to disguise his appearance.
Next, the investigator and the survivor visit the only living person on the list, the listed man.
When they arrive, they are told by the listed man's invalid twin brother, the twin, that the listed man died of a heart attack several years earlier.
They leave disappointed, assuming everyone on the list is dead.
That night, however, the twin sees and recognizes the masked murderer, who pursues him, knocks him out and pushes him into the river, drowning him.
The following day, his mother tells the investigator that “the twin” was actually the listed man, who impersonated his deceased brother for his disability pension.
From the listed man's mother, and from the widow of another person of the list, the investigator and the survivor establish that all were in the same prisoner-of-war camp in an eastern country.
A Canadian sergeant betrayed his fellow prisoners, foiling their escape attempt.
They conclude the Canadian is the murderer, and killed each person on the list to prevent them from identifying him.
They deduce that he is about to come into prominence and cannot risk being recognized.

Almost by accident, the author's final clue falls into place; it is revealed that the Canadian stands in line to an inheritance of the noble family (pronounced "the shortened name"), the lady's family of landed gentry, who avidly engage in fox hunting.

Having killed all possible witnesses to his wartime treachery, the Canadian, the claimant (pronounced 'the shortened name'), appears at a noble family estate fox hunt and introduces himself as a member of the family (the claimant has previously been seen only in disguise).
It becomes clear to the investigator and the survivor that the claimant's next victim is the lady's son, the boy, who comes before the claimant in inheriting the family title and estate.
In an attempt to divert the claimant, the investigator informs him of his investigation of the author's list, calculating to set himself up as the claimant's next victim.
That night, the claimant, who leaves for a phony meeting in the capital, sabotages the next morning's hunt by laying a drag over the fields.
He marks a blind spot behind a high wall, and positions a hay tedder where the investigator (who has the honor of leading the hunt) will be impaled upon its lethal tines.
Early the next morning, a farmer repositions the tedder.
The hunt comes to a halt at the specified spot.

The investigator reveals to the gathered crowd that he discovered and removed the hay-tedder booby trap earlier that morning and, with the help of the lead fox hound, will detect the scent of the culprit in a group protesting against the hunt.
The claimant, once again disguised, is identified and mounts the boy's horse, which was a gift from the author to the boy and trained by Romanian gypsies, to escape.
However, the boy shouts a command in Romanian, and the horse stops short, throwing the claimant and impaling him on the machine he intended for the investigator.
An American physicist and rocket scientist is travelling to a conference in the northern capital with his assistant and fiancée.
The physicist receives a radiogram to pick up a book in the northern capital; it contains a message which says, "Contact in case of emergency."
He tells the assistant he is going to another capital, but she discovers he is flying to the communist capital and follows him.
When they land, he is welcomed by representatives of the communist state's government.

The assistant realizes that the physicist has defected and is appalled that, given the circumstances of the standoff between the great powers, if she stays with him, she will likely never see her home or family again.

The physicist visits a contact, a "farmer", where it is revealed that his defection is in fact a ruse to gain the confidence of the communist state's scientific establishment in order to learn how much their chief scientist and, by extension, the allied superpower know about anti-missile systems.
The physicist has made preparations to return to his own side via an escape network known as.
However, he is followed to the farm by his appointed chaperone, a secret police officer of the communist state.

The chaperone realizes what is and that the physicist is a double agent, and as the chaperone is calling the police, a tortuous struggle commences that ends with the chaperone being killed by the physicist and the farmer's wife.
The chaperone and his motorcycle are buried on the land.
The taxicab driver who drove the physicist to the farm, however, had also seen the chaperone arrive.
When he sees the chaperone reported missing in the newspaper, he contacts the police.

Visiting the physics faculty of the university in a provincial city the next day, the physicist's interview with the scientists ends abruptly when he is questioned by security officials about the missing chaperone.

The faculty try to interrogate the assistant about her knowledge of the American classified anti-missile program, but she refuses to cooperate and runs from the room, even though she has agreed to defect to the communist state.
The physicist catches up with her to confide his actual motives and asks her to go along with the ruse.
The physicist finally goads the chief scientist into revealing his anti-missile equations in a pique over what the chief scientist believes are the physicist's mathematical mistakes.

When the chief scientist hears over the university's loudspeaker system that the physicist and the assistant are being sought for questioning, he realizes that he has given up his secrets while learning nothing in return.
The physicist and the assistant escape from the school with the help of the university clinic physician.
Pursued by the secret police, the couple travel to the communist capital, led by a guide in a decoy bus operated by the network.

Roadblocks, highway robbery by deserters from the allied superpower's army, and bunching with the "real" bus result in the police becoming aware of the deception, and everyone aboard is forced to flee.
While they are looking for a certain post office, the two encounter an exiled Polish countess, who leads them there in hopes of being sponsored for an American visa.
When they are spotted, the countess trips the pursuing guard, allowing the physicist and the assistant to escape to their next destination.
Two men approach them on the pavement, one of whom is the "farmer".
He gives them tickets to the ballet as part of a plan to smuggle them to the neutral country that evening inside the ballet troupe's luggage.

Attending the ballet featuring a famous composer's symphonic poem and waiting to be picked up, they are spotted and reported to the police by the lead ballerina, who flew to the communist capital on the same airplane as the physicist.
The physicist and the assistant escape through the crowd after shouting "fire".
An aide hides them in two hampers of costumes, and they are ferried across the sea to the neutral country on a freighter of the communist state.
The ballerina, who is also on board, sees the aide speak to two hampers as they are lifted onto the pier.
She informs the guards and the hampers are shot with a machine gun.
It is then revealed that the physicist and the assistant were in two different hampers.
The aide had noticed the ballerina's suspicions and had intentionally spoken to the wrong hampers, so that the three could swim to shore during the commotion.
They safely arrive in the neutral country.
Wealthy eccentric the host hires struggling actor the young man as his personal secretary to play a "practical joke".

Pretending to be on his deathbed, the host invites three former lovers to his canal-city palazzo for a final visit: penniless the princess, fading movie star the screen actress, and southern-state millionairess the wealthy guest.
Accompanying the wealthy guest is her nurse, the companion.

Each of the three former lovers brings the host a valuable timepiece as a present: the wealthy guest's, an elaborate porcelain antique; the screen actress's, a large quartz block with clock faces telling global time; and the princess's, an heirloom hourglass reputedly filled with precious gold powder.

The young man soon recognizes that the premise of the "practical joke" is based on the plot of an old playwright's 17th Century theater classic the old comedy, in which a swindler poses as a dying man to dupe three men who aspire to inherit his fortune, each bearing luxurious gifts.
A former law student, the young man begins to suspect the motives behind the "practical joke" and to question how his role may incur legal liability.
The three former lovers warily size each other up.
The wealthy guest boldly announces she is the host's common-law wife, and the others can expect to inherit nothing.
The companion goes on a late-night date with the young man, during which the young man leaves her alone at a restaurant for over an hour ostensibly to make an important phone inquiry.
On her return, the companion finds the wealthy guest dead of an overdose of sleeping pills, an apparent suicide.
However, the companion knows that the pills the wealthy guest had been taking were placebos—harmless fakes.
The police inspector investigates.
The young man reveals to the companion that the host is perpetrating a charade and the final joke was to be the reading of the will, empowering the young man to choose the heir.
On searching the young man's room, the companion finds several quarters from the wealthy guest’s missing roll of change.
She suspects the young man of murdering the wealthy guest and plotting to kill the host.
When the companion confronts the young man, he locks her in her room, telling her it is for her own safety.
She manages to escape via a dumbwaiter to warn the host, informing him that she has already confronted the young man.
The host's displeased reaction puzzles her.
He sends her back to her room.
The next morning, the host is found dead.

The princess, the screen actress, and the inspector attend a reading of the host's will, in which the young man is assigned as the executor with the power to fill in the blank left for the heir’s name.
Divulging the host's scheme based on the old comedy, the young man reveals that the host killed the wealthy guest.
The host had lost the quarters the companion found in the young man's room to the young man during a poker game—the host's greed couldn't resist taking petty change.
Despite his fabulous but heavily mortgaged palazzo, the host was broke.
As the wealthy guest's common-law husband, the host plotted to inherit her immense fortune.
Once the young man had figured it out, informing the companion, the host realized he would be arrested for the wealthy guest’s murder and chose suicide.
As a final disdainful act, the host had shattered the timepieces given to him by the three women.
The princess's hourglass is found empty of its gold dust.
Taking out the centers of bonbons from a box of chocolates, and filling the bonbons with the gold dust, the host swallowed the hourglass's entire contents.
The inspector asks why the host would have done this, and the young man suddenly realizes that the host has found a way to "take a fortune with him" after death.
The princess now announces that the contents of the hourglass—a mere facsimile of the original—was inexpensive pyrite, or "fool's gold."
The host's spirit, as a voice-over, expresses resentment that the princess has cheapened his parting gesture.
The companion "whimsically" asks the young man to write her name down in the will as the heir of the host's estate as a souvenir, with the inspector signing as a witness.
After the young man complies, an amused inspector compliments the young man on his generosity.
The wealthy guest's estate is so vast that even after the host's debts are paid, the companion will still emerge an extremely wealthy woman.
The companion informs the indignant young man that she will marry him and hand over the money once he resumes his law studies and becomes a lawyer.
The host's spirit now expresses admiration for "the Anglo-Saxon woman" for "the larceny" the companion serendipitously has managed to pull off.
In 1880, an unknown drifter and gambler in the small frontier town, 100 miles (161 km) from the big city in the western state, is caught cheating at a five-card stud poker game.
The players, led by the volatile ringleader, take the cheating gambler to lynch him.
One of the players, the objector, tries to prevent the others from administering frontier justice, but is unable to stop the hanging.
The objector leaves town, but later returns, when he hears that several of the other players from the poker game have become victims of grisly murders.
The objector starts a relationship with the lady barber, the barbershop owner.
The town has a new resident, a stern and somewhat edgy revolver-carrying evangelical preacher, named the reverend.
As more members of the lynch mob are killed off one by one by strangling, it becomes clear that someone is taking revenge, and it is up to the objector to solve the mystery.
The ringleader is shown to be the one telling the reverend who was at the game and involved in killing the stranger, who is the reverend's brother.
The ringleader tells the reverend falsely that the innocent player was involved, the reverend kills the innocent player.

As the innocent player is dying he puts his hands together like he is praying, the objector knows that the innocent player never prayed, thus realizes that the reverend is the murderer, and he kills the reverend in a shootout.
Last scene is with the objector and the lady barber as the objector rides off to the big city and the lady barber is going to follow him in a week.

After the missing executive, a chemical company executive from one state, disappears, the police find an obscene letter in his office addressed to a call girl in the big city, who had received several such letters.
After six months of fruitless police work, the colleague, a fellow executive at the missing executive's company, hires a family friend and detective to investigate the disappearance.
The detective rents an apartment in the basement of the call girl's building, taps her phone, and follows her as she turns tricks.
The call girl appears to enjoy the freedom of freelancing as a call girl while auditioning for acting and modeling jobs, but she reveals the emptiness of her life to her psychiatrist.
After learning that the detective has been watching her, the call girl says that she does not recognize the missing executive.
She acknowledges having been beaten up by a john two years earlier but cannot identify the missing executive from a photo.
She further admits to the detective that she is a nervous and paranoid person.
The call girl takes the detective to meet her former pimp, who had managed the first woman, a prostitute who had referred the abusive client to the call girl.
The first woman has apparently committed suicide, and their other colleague, the second woman, has since become a drug addict and disappeared.
The detective and the call girl develop a romance, although she tells her psychiatrist that she wishes their relationship would end because she felt more in control of herself when turning tricks.
They find the second woman, who tells them that the photo of the missing executive is not that of the client, who was an older man.
The second woman's body is later found in the river.
The detective connects the apparent suicides of the two prostitutes, surmising that the client was using the missing executive's name.
He also thinks the client killed the missing executive and might kill the call girl next.
The detective revisits the missing executive's acquaintances.
By typographic comparison, the obscene letters are traced to the colleague, to whom the detective has been reporting during his investigation.
The detective asks the colleague for money to buy the "black book" of the first woman's clients to learn the identity of the abusive client.
He leaves enough bread crumbs to see whether the colleague reveals his own complicity in the murders.
The colleague follows the call girl to a client's office and reveals that he sent her the letters.

He tells her that after the missing executive accidentally found him physically abusing the first woman, the colleague was worried that the missing executive would use the incident to sabotage the colleague's career, so he tried to frame the missing executive by planting the letter in his office.
After playing a snuff audiotape he recorded as he murdered the second woman, he attacks the call girl.
When he sees the detective rush in, the colleague lurches backward, crashing through a window to his death.
The call girl vacates her apartment with the detective's help.

A voiceover conversation with her psychiatrist reveals her hesitancy to surrender her life of autonomy to enter a traditional relationship with the detective, saying that she would lose her mind if she turned to a domestic lifestyle.
She admits that, although she will miss the detective, she is unable to tell him and jokes that the doctor will likely see her again the next week.
As they leave the apartment, the call girl receives a telephone call from a client and informs him she is leaving the big city and does not expect to return.
She and the detective leave the apartment together.
A handsome young artist arrives at his newly inherited estate with his beautiful wife.
They meet the housekeeper and the caretaker.
The artist happens upon a 19th-century portrait of a blonde woman with captivating green eyes that seem to mesmerize him.
The housekeeper informs him that the woman is a former lady of the estate, who had lived there over 100 years earlier.
The couple's friends, two married novelists who have co-written several successful horror novels, move into a cottage on the estate.

The artist soon begins to be troubled by startling visions and haunting dreams about one of his ancestors, and his ancestor's mistress, the woman in the portrait—who had been hanged as a witch in a past century.

The housekeeper eventually reveals to the artist that she is the reincarnation of a little girl who had lived at the estate over 150 years ago, and that the artist himself is the reincarnation of the ancestor.

The ancestor had had an affair with the woman in the portrait, wife of his brother, resulting in her being hanged—and the ancestor being sealed alive in the family crypt with the woman in the portrait's corpse.
On a trip to the big city, the two novelists discover a painting of the ancestor, which bears an uncanny resemblance to the artist.
Convinced that their friends are in grave danger, the couple hurry home to the estate, where they are attacked by the ghost of the woman in the portrait.
Meanwhile, the artist has become possessed by the spirit of the ancestor, and attempts to drown the young wife in a disused swimming pool on the estate.
The two novelists arrive in time to revive her, but the artist, having no memory of his actions, refuses to believe their wild tale.
The housekeeper and the caretaker conspire to eliminate the artist's loved ones.
The artist, seeing the scratches on his wrist where the young wife had tried to fend him off, realizes the truth of the male novelist's warning and rushes to rescue his friends.
The caretaker has managed to take the young wife prisoner (despite his having been shot in the face by the female novelist), and the artist fights with him high atop a train trestle.
As the caretaker slashes the artist's cheek with a knife, creating a gash in his left cheek that looks remarkably like the one the ancestor had, the young wife rushes to try to save her husband.
She strikes the caretaker with a nearby plank, knocking him off the artist and onto the edge of the trestle.
He teeters on the edge for a moment, then plunges to his death after the young wife pushes him.
The group rush back to the estate to confront the housekeeper.
As they arrive, she jumps from the top of the house when she sees the ghostly woman in the portrait beckon her from below.
In the end, the two couples prepare to leave the estate forever.
The two novelists leave first, with the artist and the young wife following.
However, instead of driving away, the artist returns to the house, saying he intends to retrieve some canvases.
When he fails to come back, the young wife follows, only to find him now completely possessed by the ancestor.
The woman in the portrait enters the room, reborn in the flesh.
The camera freezes on the young wife's face as she begins to scream, as the artist and the woman in the portrait advance on her.
A press agency news wire shown at the end reveals that the two novelists have been killed in a car accident.
Witnesses reported seeing a ghostly fog filling the car as it veered off the road.
At a seaside high school, female students are being targeted by a serial killer.
The boy, a male student is experiencing sexual frustration, surrounded by a seemingly unending stream of beautiful and provocative classmates.
The coach is the high school's football coach and guidance counselor, who has frequent sexual encounters with different female students.
The boy develops a crush on the substitute teacher as he presents his report on a classic poet's epic poem.
The coach tries to help the boy deal with his sexual needs by encouraging him to approach the substitute teacher.
The boy tells him he constantly has an erection when talking to an attractive woman.
The coach talks to the substitute teacher and recommends that she teach the boy to build confidence, telling her he's impotent.
The substitute teacher takes the boy home after school and arouses him by reading the poet's poetry.
The boy hides in the closet, but the substitute teacher tells him that she knows about his sexual problem and wants to help.
Seeing his erection through his trousers, she reports to the coach in school the next day that she believes she's made progress.
The coach urges the substitute teacher to be more aggressive at their next meeting.
The boy visits the substitute teacher and gifts her a liquor-filled chocolate duck, then becomes nervous and leaves.
When he returns to retrieve his keys, he finds the substitute teacher in a sexy nightgown.
They kiss passionately and have sex.
A detective of the state police, investigating the murders, suspects the coach is the killer.
The boy finds evidence against the coach in his office.
The coach confesses to the boy on a pier, then drives his car into the ocean.
When his body is never recovered, the detective suspects that the coach has faked his suicide.
After the coach's memorial service, a much more confident boy flirts with several female students, taking one for a ride on his motorcycle.
The pathologist is the new pathologist at a city hospital.
He befriends his colleagues and falls in love with a dietitian.
The hospital is run by the chief surgeon.
Police are investigating a series of morphine thefts at the hospital.
One night, the chief surgeon's daughter dies in the emergency room after a botched abortion.
A fellow doctor is arrested for performing the abortion.
The pathologist pretends to be his lawyer in order to visit him in jail.
The fellow doctor admits to charging $25 for illegal abortions, because he was horrified at how women suffered at the hands of amateurs.
However, the fellow doctor says he did not perform the daughter's abortion.
The police captain warns the pathologist to leave the case alone, but the pathologist hates the idea of his innocent friend going to prison.
The post-mortem reveals that whoever did the procedure had curettage knowledge but pierced the endometrium, causing the fatal hemorrhaging.
The daughter's blood work shows she was not pregnant.
The pathologist suspects she missed a few periods and panicked into getting an abortion.
He questions the daughter's roommate.
She confesses that she hated the daughter for stealing her boyfriend.
The pathologist visits the boyfriend at the massage parlor where he works.
He sees a nurse leaving as he arrives.
The pathologist deduces that the nurse was stealing the hospital's drugs for the boyfriend to sell.
He gets the nurse to confess to performing the abortion to fund her drug habit.
The boyfriend goes berserk and tries to kill the pathologist multiple times before the police captain kills him.
